# Brusselator

`brusselator` · *Prigogine & Lefever, 1968*

## Introduction

The Brusselator is a set of four chemical reactions whose concentrations can
oscillate for ever instead of settling down. Only two of its species change, called `X` and `Y`. Feed it
steadily and, depending on one knob, it either comes to rest at a fixed
mixture or keeps cycling: `X` builds up slowly, then shoots up and crashes,
again and again, with the same period and the same amplitude whatever the
starting point. Such a self-sustained cycle is called a *limit cycle*.

It was proposed by Ilya Prigogine and René Lefever of the Université Libre de
Bruxelles in 1968, in a paper about *dissipative
structures*: order that appears in chemical systems kept far from
thermodynamic equilibrium by a constant flow of matter. Their question was
which kinds of reactions can make a uniform, steady chemical mixture unstable.
Their answer was that it takes autocatalysis, a species that speeds up its own
production. The Brusselator is their simplest example. The authors called its
key step, in which three molecules must meet at once, "physically
unrealistic", but kept it because the model then has only two changing
species and the mathematics stays simple. Their paper was mainly about
patterns in space (with diffusion); it also noted that such schemes can
oscillate in time.

It is a simulation model in the plainest sense: a fixed list of reactions with
mass-action rates, meant to be written as differential equations and solved.
Nothing in it is constructive: no new species ever appear. Banzhaf and
Yamamoto use it in their chapter on computing with chemistries (book §17.4.2)
as an early model of a *biochemical oscillator*, the kind of circuit that
could give a clock signal to a synthetic chemical computer, in the same way a
clock paces an electronic circuit. It sits next to
[Okamoto's biochemical switch](okamoto-switch.md) in that section. Among the
catalog's other oscillators, the [Oregonator](oregonator.md) models a real
chemical oscillator (the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction), the
[Repressilator](repressilator.md) one built from genes in bacteria, and
[Lotka–Volterra](lotka-volterra.md) circles a fixed point on orbits that
depend on where it starts, rather than on a single limit cycle. The book also
mentions the Brusselator as something [ARMS](arms.md), a multiset rewriting
system, can model; that entry has a `system="brusselator"` option with the
same four rules.

## How it works

### The four reactions

```
A -> X            (k1)  X is fed in from the reservoir A
B + X -> Y + D    (k2)  B converts X into Y, releasing waste D
2 X + Y -> 3 X    (k3)  two X turn a Y into a third X: autocatalysis
X -> E            (k4)  X decays into waste E
```

Each `k` is a *rate constant*. Under *mass action* a reaction runs at a speed
equal to its rate constant times the product of its reactant concentrations,
so `2 X + Y -> 3 X` runs at `k3 × [X]² × [Y]` (square brackets mean
concentration).

The book describes the roles as follows: `X` is an autocatalytic enzyme that
makes more of itself from the substrate `Y` (reaction 3); `B` partly reverses
this by forcing `X` to release `Y` (reaction 2); `X` is injected steadily
(reaction 1) and decays (reaction 4). `D` and `E` are waste: they are made but
never used again, so they do not affect the dynamics.

`A` and `B` are *buffered*: their concentrations are held at fixed values `a`
and `b`, as if a reservoir topped them up whenever a reaction used some. This
is what keeps the system open and away from equilibrium. Chemart's generator
lists them in `net.extras["buffered"]`; whatever simulates the network must
keep them constant.

### Why it oscillates

Follow one cycle. When `X` is scarce, the autocatalytic step is slow (its
speed goes as `[X]²`), so `B` converts the `X` that trickles in into `Y`, and
`Y` piles up. Once `X` has grown enough, the autocatalytic step, fed by all
that stored `Y`, takes off: `X` grows faster the more there is of it, and
`Y` is used up in a burst. With `Y` gone, the autocatalysis stops; `X` is
drained by reactions 2 and 4, and `Y` starts accumulating again.

Whether this cycle dies out or keeps going depends on the balance between the
feed and the feedback. With all rate constants equal to 1, the two changing
species obey

```
d[X]/dt = a − b[X] + [X]²[Y] − [X]
d[Y]/dt =     b[X] − [X]²[Y]
```

Setting both to zero gives the single *steady state* `[X] = a`, `[Y] = b/a`,
where production and consumption balance (Prigogine and Lefever give the same
state, their eq. 4.2). The book states that this state is stable when
`b < 1 + a²` and that sustained oscillations occur when `b > 1 + a²`. Below
the threshold a disturbance dies away in damped oscillations; above it the
system is pushed away from the steady state onto the limit cycle. The switch
from one behaviour to the other as `b` crosses `1 + a²` is called a *Hopf
bifurcation*. With `a = 1` the threshold is `b = 2`.

For general rate constants the same algebra gives the steady state
`[X] = k1·a/k4`, `[Y] = k2·k4·b / (k1·k3·a)`, and the standard linear
stability analysis moves the threshold to
`b = (k4 + k3·k1²·a²/k4²) / k2`. These two formulas are derived here from the
rate equations, not quoted from the book; the run under "Using it" checks one
case.

### The reactor

The book integrates the rate equations numerically (an *ODE*, ordinary
differential equation, model). The same network can also be run as a
*stochastic simulation* (the Gillespie algorithm): individual reaction events
at random times, with molecule counts instead of concentrations. For that the
rate constants `k` must be converted into per-molecule constants `c`, and the
three-molecule step needs care: its constant carries a factor `2!` because
two of its three reactants are the same species. Chemart supplies the
conversion as `chemart.kinetics.k_to_c`.

Chemart itself only generates the network. It does not run either reactor;
the examples below integrate or simulate the generated network with a few
lines of NumPy and SciPy.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). A, B (buffered), X, Y (dynamic), D, E (waste)

**R — reactions** (*explicit* — listed reaction by reaction; molecules per reaction: 1, 2, 3). A --k1--&gt; X ; B + X --k2--&gt; Y + D ; 2X + Y --k3--&gt; 3X ; X --k4--&gt; E

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time); or `ssa` (stochastic simulation (Gillespie): individual reaction events happen at random times).

*How the population is bounded:* A and B held constant by buffering

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("brusselator", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
brusselator: 6 species, 4 reactions, status=complete
provides: catalysts, initial-state, rate-constants, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
extras: buffered
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
A -> X  [mass-action k=1.0]
B + X -> Y + D  [mass-action k=1.0]
2 X + Y -> 3 X  [mass-action k=1.0]
X -> E  [mass-action k=1.0]
```

The default call above gives the network of the book's figure 17.6 (left):
`a = 1`, `b = 3`, every rate constant 1, and `X`, `Y`, `D`, `E` starting at 0
in `net.initial_state`. The four reactions are exactly the book's reactions
17.14 to 17.17, and `net.extras` has a single field, `buffered`, naming `A`
and `B`. The network involves no randomness, so the `seed` changes nothing.

#### Reproducing figure 17.6

The book's figure shows `b = 3` (oscillating) next to `b = 1.7` (damped). This
script integrates the generated network, holding the buffered species fixed:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

import chemart


def simulate(net, t_end, n=6001):
    ids, R, P = net.matrices()
    R = R.toarray()
    S = (P.toarray() - R).astype(float)
    k = np.array([r.rate["k"] for r in net.reactions])
    held = [ids.index(s) for s in net.extras["buffered"]]
    x0 = np.array([net.initial_state[s] for s in ids])

    def f(t, x):
        v = k * np.prod(x[:, None] ** R, axis=0)  # mass action
        dx = S @ v
        dx[held] = 0.0  # A and B are buffered
        return dx

    t = np.linspace(0, t_end, n)
    sol = solve_ivp(f, (0, t_end), x0, t_eval=t, rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12)
    return t, dict(zip(ids, sol.y))


for b in (3.0, 1.7):
    net = chemart.generate_network("brusselator", b=b)
    t, x = simulate(net, 60)
    late = t >= 40
    X, Y = x["X"][late], x["Y"][late]
    print(f"b={b}: t in [40, 60]: X from {X.min():.2f} to {X.max():.2f}, "
          f"Y from {Y.min():.2f} to {Y.max():.2f}")
```

```
b=3.0: t in [40, 60]: X from 0.37 to 3.75, Y from 0.85 to 4.72
b=1.7: t in [40, 60]: X from 1.00 to 1.00, Y from 1.70 to 1.70
```

At `b = 3` the concentrations are still swinging widely after 40 time units.
At `b = 1.7`, `X` rose to a peak of 1.37 early on and has settled at the
steady state `(a, b/a) = (1, 1.7)`.

#### Crossing the threshold

To see the threshold, run each setting to `t = 400` with the same `simulate`
and measure the swing of `X` (maximum minus minimum) over the last 100 time
units. A swing of zero means the run has settled at the steady state:

```python
for params in ({"b": 1.9}, {"b": 2.1}, {"b": 2.5}, {"b": 3.0}, {"b": 4.0},
               {"a": 2.0, "b": 4.5}, {"a": 2.0, "b": 5.5},
               {"k3": 2.0, "b": 2.8}, {"k3": 2.0, "b": 3.2}):
    t, x = simulate(chemart.generate_network("brusselator", **params), 400, n=40001)
    X = x["X"][t >= 300]
    print(params, f"X swing {np.ptp(X):.3f}, final (X, Y) = ({x['X'][-1]:.3f}, {x['Y'][-1]:.3f})")
```

```
{'b': 1.9} X swing 0.000, final (X, Y) = (1.000, 1.900)
{'b': 2.1} X swing 0.764, final (X, Y) = (1.473, 1.657)
{'b': 2.5} X swing 2.018, final (X, Y) = (0.493, 3.119)
{'b': 3.0} X swing 3.381, final (X, Y) = (0.403, 4.119)
{'b': 4.0} X swing 6.177, final (X, Y) = (3.157, 4.562)
{'a': 2.0, 'b': 4.5} X swing 0.000, final (X, Y) = (2.000, 2.250)
{'a': 2.0, 'b': 5.5} X swing 3.359, final (X, Y) = (3.985, 1.340)
{'k3': 2.0, 'b': 2.8} X swing 0.000, final (X, Y) = (1.000, 1.400)
{'k3': 2.0, 'b': 3.2} X swing 0.973, final (X, Y) = (1.605, 1.049)
```

With `a = 1` the cycle appears between `b = 1.9` and `b = 2.1`, as
`1 + a² = 2` predicts, and grows as `b` increases. It also slows down: in a
separate run, the mean time between peaks of `X` was about 6.3 time units at
`b = 2.1` and about 9.0 at `b = 4`. With `a = 2` the threshold moves to 5,
and the steady state below it is `(2, 4.5/2) = (2, 2.25)`. With `k3 = 2` the
general formula puts the threshold at `b = 3` and the steady state at
`(1, b/2)`, which is what the runs show. Each setting takes one to two seconds.

#### A stochastic run

To simulate molecule by molecule, choose how many molecules make one unit of
concentration (`omega` below, standing for Avogadro's number times the
volume) and convert each rate constant with `k_to_c`:

```python
from math import comb

import numpy as np

import chemart
from chemart.kinetics import k_to_c

net = chemart.generate_network("brusselator", seed=1)  # a = 1, b = 3
omega = 200  # N_A * V: molecules per unit concentration
held = set(net.extras["buffered"])
n = {s: round(c * omega) for s, c in net.initial_state.items()}  # A = 200, B = 600
c = [k_to_c(r.rate["k"], r.reactants, volume=omega, avogadro=1.0) for r in net.reactions]
print("c:", [round(v, 8) for v in c])

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
t, t_end, events = 0.0, 60.0, 0
samples = []
while t < t_end:
    # propensity = c * number of distinct reactant combinations
    a = np.array([ci * np.prod([comb(n[s], m) for s, m in r.reactants.items()])
                  for ci, r in zip(c, net.reactions)])
    total = a.sum()
    t += rng.exponential(1 / total)
    r = net.reactions[rng.choice(len(a), p=a / total)]
    for s, m in r.reactants.items():
        if s not in held:
            n[s] -= m
    for s, m in r.products.items():
        if s not in held:
            n[s] += m
    events += 1
    if t >= 40:
        samples.append(n["X"] / omega)
print(f"{events} events; X/omega over t 40-60: {min(samples):.2f} to {max(samples):.2f}")
```

```
c: [1.0, 0.005, 5e-05, 1.0]
87573 events; X/omega over t 40-60: 0.24 to 4.68
```

The third constant is `2 / omega²`: the `1/omega²` for a three-molecule
reaction, times the `2!` for the repeated `X`. The noisy run follows the
same cycle as the ODE (compare `X` from 0.37 to 3.75 above), with extra
scatter from the small molecule numbers. It takes about eight seconds; the
number of events, and so the time, grows in proportion to `omega`.

The parameter table below lists the six parameters: the two buffered
concentrations and the four rate constants.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `a` | `float` | `1.0` | population | [A], held constant <br>≥ `0` |
| `b` | `float` | `3.0` | population | [B], held constant; sustained oscillations require b &gt; 1 + a^2 when all k_i = 1 <br>≥ `0` |
| `k1` | `float` | `1.0` | kinetic | A -&gt; X <br>≥ `0` |
| `k2` | `float` | `1.0` | kinetic | B + X -&gt; Y + D <br>≥ `0` |
| `k3` | `float` | `1.0` | kinetic | 2X + Y -&gt; 3X <br>≥ `0` |
| `k4` | `float` | `1.0` | kinetic | X -&gt; E <br>≥ `0` |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "1 decision"

    - Buffered species A and B are listed in extras.buffered: their concentrations stay at a and b although the reactions consume them. Initial X, Y, D, E are 0, as in figure 17.6.

## Results

**The model's origin.** Prigogine and Lefever (1968) introduced the scheme as
the first of three reaction schemes that can make a steady chemical state
unstable, and the one they analysed in detail because it has only two
intermediate species. Their main result concerns space, not time. With
diffusion added, they derived the critical value of `B` at which the uniform
steady state becomes unstable to disturbances of a particular wavelength, a
*symmetry-breaking* instability of the kind Turing had described in 1952. They
then studied the simplest spatial case, two connected boxes. With `A = 2` and
both diffusion coefficients equal to 1, the uniform state becomes unstable at
`B = 9`; beyond it a second, non-uniform steady state exists, with more `Y`
and less `X` in one box than in the other, which they found stable for
`9.8 ≤ B ≤ 11.2`. They offered it as "a striking example of a dissipative
structure". In a short final part on oscillations ("rotations" around the
steady state), they concluded that autocatalytic or cross-catalytic steps are
necessary for oscillation, and that all their schemes oscillate for some range
of the constraints. Chemart has no diffusion or compartments for this entry,
so it reproduces none of the spatial results.

**The oscillation threshold, reproduced.** The book (§17.4.2, figure 17.6)
states that sustained oscillations occur for `b > 1 + a²` when every rate
constant is 1, and shows `a = 1` with `b = 3` (sustained) and `b = 1.7`
(damped, converging to a steady state). This is the entry's one catalogued
phenomenon: limit-cycle oscillations above the threshold and damped
oscillations to `(X, Y) = (a, b/a)` below it. Chemart reproduces it. The test
`test_brusselator_oscillates_only_above_hopf` in
`tests/chemistries/test_w1_dynamics.py` integrates the generated network and
checks that at `b = 3` the range of `X` between `t = 40` and `t = 60` exceeds
1, and that at `b = 1.7` the state reaches `X = 1`, `Y = 1.7` within 0.1%
by `t = 300`. The runs above show the same, and locate the threshold between
`b = 1.9` and `b = 2.1`.

**Stochastic kinetics.** The catalog lists the Gillespie algorithm as a
possible reactor, and the stochastic run above shows the conversion working
for the three-molecule step. No test checks this: the tests of `k_to_c` cover
only one- and two-molecule reactions.

**Later use.** The book calls the Brusselator an idealized theoretical model
and notes that such models "are widespread in the literature, since they
simplify the mathematical analysis of the resulting dynamical system, while
capturing the essential qualitative phenomena of interest." Its
reaction-diffusion form is still studied by mathematicians: Yao and Wang
(2015), for example, call it "the famous diffusive Brusselator model" and
prove that it supports spatio-temporal standing waves, not only the uniform
oscillation that appears at the Hopf bifurcation. In artificial chemistry,
Suzuki and Tanaka (1998) wrote the four reactions as rewriting rules in ARMS
and reported Brusselator-like oscillations; the [ARMS](arms.md) page explains
why Chemart does not reproduce those.

**A note on numbering.** Prigogine and Lefever list the reactions in a
different order (`A → X`, `2X + Y → 3X`, `B + X → Y + D`, `X → E`), and
their rate equations attach `k2` to the three-molecule step and `k3` to
`B + X`. Chemart follows the book's order and numbering, so its `k2` is the
paper's `k3` and vice versa. With all constants equal to 1 the difference
disappears.

## References

Banzhaf, W. & Yamamoto, L. (2015). *Artificial Chemistries*. MIT Press. Section 17.4.2, 19.3; ARMS 9.4; the book's bibliography entries [675].

### Further reading

- Prigogine, I. & Lefever, R. (1968). Symmetry breaking instabilities in
  dissipative systems. II. *Journal of Chemical Physics* 48(4), 1695–1700.
  <https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1668896>. The original paper (book reference
  [675]); the Brusselator is its "Scheme I".
- Yao, J. & Wang, X. (2015). Oscillation and instability in chemical
  reactions. arXiv:1510.00891. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00891>
- Lefever, R. & Nicolis, G. (1971). Chemical instabilities and sustained
  oscillations. *Journal of Theoretical Biology* 30, 267–284. An early
  follow-up from the Brussels group, cited by Yao and Wang; not read for this
  page.
- Suzuki, Y. & Tanaka, H. (1998). Order parameter for a symbolic chemical
  system. In *Artificial Life VI*, pp. 130–139, MIT Press. The Brusselator
  as ARMS rewriting rules (their fig. 8).

The book's §9.4 (on ARMS) says that chapter 19 discusses the Brusselator in
more detail, and the section list above includes 19.3. In the
book's text the Brusselator is treated only in §17.4.2; chapter 19 covers the
Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction and the Repressilator instead.
